research.interest: Tasting whisky deliberately and remembering what I actually liked
research.desired_outcome: Choose the next pour and the next bottle from my own palate evidence instead of strangers' ratings
practice: Pour a dram, nose it, taste it, and note nose, palate, and finish while the glass is still in hand
Keep a shelf of sealed, open, and finished bottles with what each cost and how full it is
Compare regions, cask types, and peat levels to learn what the palate actually returns to
constraints: capture works one-handed with a glass in the other
original wording of notes is kept verbatim
useful offline in a dim room
open_questions: whether bar pours and samples belong on the shelf
whether bottles are shared with a club
usage_context: desktop when planning the next purchase
research.first_value: Record one dram and see it join that bottle's story with your own words kept verbatim

evidence.claim: Serious whisky tracking separates the distillery, the bottling, and the individual bottle, each with stable identity.
Community tasting notes are structured as nose, palate, and finish with an overall score, not one free-text blob.
Stable identities and relationships should be explicit and enforceable rather than repeated as text fields.
A dram is an observation of a bottle at a time; corrections preserve the original record.
Indexes should follow concrete filtering, joining, and ordering workloads.
Begin with user needs and real context, then do the hard work required to make the service simple.
Keyboard access, focus, reflow, labels, status, and error recovery are release requirements.

concepts.title: The Shelf Wall
concepts.thesis: Make the collection itself the interface and keep tasting a light annotation on top of it.
concepts.primary_loop: Add a bottle, watch fill levels drop, and browse the wall by region and cask.
concepts.primary_affordance: A photographic shelf of bottle silhouettes with live fill levels
concepts.differentiator: Fastest way to answer what is open and what to buy next

concepts.title: Tasting Bench
concepts.thesis: Capture the dram while it is in the glass and let every pour deepen one bottle's story.
concepts.primary_loop: Pour, note nose then palate then finish, score it, and close the app before the glass is empty.
concepts.primary_affordance: A tri-panel nose/palate/finish dram card with descriptor chips
concepts.differentiator: The only concept that works one-handed mid-dram without losing structure
tradeoffs: analysis arrives only after drams accumulate

concepts.title: Palate Atlas
concepts.thesis: Treat every tagged descriptor as a data point and draw the drinker's actual palate over time.
concepts.primary_loop: Tag descriptors on each dram, watch the constellation form, and pick the next bottle from a gap in the map.
concepts.primary_affordance: A descriptor constellation linked back to bottles and regions
concepts.differentiator: Turns scattered notes into an explicit personal flavor map
tradeoffs: needs disciplined tagging before it pays off

relationships.description: Every bottle names its producer once.
Every dram is poured from one bottle.
Descriptors belong to the dram they were tasted in.

constraints.reason: Bottled whisky strength stays within physical limits.
Scores stay on the drinker's declared 100-point scale.
A bottle cannot be finished before it is opened.

The palate map groups descriptors across all drams.
Tonight's answer filters to open bottles by remaining fill.

workloads.question: What is open tonight and how full is each bottle?
workloads.acceptance: The open shelf answers in one glance with fill levels and regions visible.

workloads.question: How has this bottle tasted across its drams, and is the score drifting?
workloads.acceptance: Every dram's verbatim notes and score line up chronologically with serving style visible.

workloads.question: Which descriptors keep recurring in drams scored 85 or higher?
workloads.expected_scale: hundreds of notes across the shelf
workloads.acceptance: Recurring descriptors surface with links back to the exact drams that earned them.

workloads.question: Which finished bottles earned a rebuy at their price?
workloads.acceptance: Finished bottles rank by the drinker's own scores beside what each cost.

temporal_policy: poured_at is the effective tasting time
corrected notes never overwrite the original wording
privacy_policy: tasting company and context stay local unless explicitly exported
prices are never shared in exports by default

visual_world.name: Dunnage Bench
visual_world.mood: Dim, warm, unhurried — a dunnage warehouse shelf lit for one glass
visual_world.typography: A quiet serif for expressions and distilleries with a humanist sans for capture and a monospaced face for ABV and scores
visual_world.color_strategy: Charred-oak darks with amber spirit accents and a cool bottle-green counterpoint; nothing neon, nothing clinical
visual_world.layout_principle: The current dram anchors the viewport; the shelf and the map unfold laterally as evidence, never as a dashboard grid
visual_world.density: Spacious during a pour, compact and aligned when comparing bottles
signature_elements: fill-level bottle silhouettes on the shelf rail
descriptor constellation that grows with every tagged note

flows.title: Record the first real dram
flows.trigger: User approves the Tasting Bench concept.

steps.action: Name the bottle, pour, and speak or type nose, palate, and finish.
steps.result: A dram receipt appears with the drinker's wording verbatim.

steps.action: Confirm or correct the interpreted serving and score.
steps.result: The canonical dram and its provenance are visible in the bottle's story.

flows.success: The user can point at tonight's dram in the bottle's story and every word is theirs.

flows.title: Choose tonight's pour
flows.trigger: More than one bottle is open.

steps.action: Scan open bottles by fill level and region.
steps.result: The shelf answers what is open without any query.

steps.action: Check which descriptors have been missing lately.
steps.result: A gap in the constellation suggests the style to pour.

flows.success: The choice is made from the drinker's own evidence, not a ratings site.

responsive_strategy: On phones the dram card's three panels stack in tasting order with the pour action fixed in reach; the shelf becomes a swipeable rail.
On desktop the bench keeps card and story side by side and the constellation gains hover detail with a full data table alternative.

release_thresholds.schema: all identity, relationship, constraint, and state-transition cases pass
release_thresholds.experience: first dram and tonight's-pour flows pass on mobile and desktop
release_thresholds.evidence: every entity and critical view has an approved derivation

derivations.decision: Separate distillery, bottle, dram, and flavor note so the producer, the object, the event, and the observation each keep their own lifecycle.
Anchor the app on the in-hand dram rather than the collection, because capture happens mid-pour.
derivations.user_decision: Capture must work one-handed with a glass in the other.

derivations.decision: Record serving style as a first-class enum because neat and highball are different drams of the same bottle.
derivations.user_decision: Serving style matters — neat, a drop of water, or a highball are different drams.

derivations.decision: Index flavor notes by descriptor and axis for the recurrence workload behind the palate map.
Use a dim dunnage-warehouse world with amber accents instead of ratings-site cards, matching where drams are actually tasted.
